argument_summary: Certification is only supportable on a narrow, caveated basis from the existing admissible record. The strongest defensible position is not that the logistics customs triage weakness is cured, but that the release otherwise met aggregate readiness, had no severity-one rehearsal incidents, and includes measured rollout, monitoring, and rollback controls, while the material limitation for tariff-code exception handling must be explicitly disclosed for that named use case. The exposed segment remains in scope, so the packet should be treated as a caveated certification argument rather than a clean compliance showing.
claims_about_business_cost: No independent business-cost claim is needed to justify the position. The governance argument should stand or fall on the admissible readiness, disclosure, and control evidence rather than on rollout-velocity considerations.
claims_about_policy: The admissible policy record cuts both ways. It supports disclosure of unresolved material limitations in named launch use cases, and public guidance supports documenting limitations and monitoring deployed risk. But the operative policy text also states that rollout controls and post-launch monitoring mitigate a material weakness only if the affected use case is excluded or covered by reviewed risk acceptance, and that a 6% rollout, dashboard, or rollback switch do not remove disclosure duties when the affected segment remains exposed. On this record, the compliant reading is therefore limited: disclosure plus controls can support a caveated certification posture, but not an unqualified claim that the weakness is resolved or fully mitigated for policy purposes.
concessions: The logistics customs triage segment is below target on tariff-code exception handling and remains eligible in the initial rollout cohort.
The current rollout gate does not exclude the affected segment.
The risk-acceptance draft is not approved and does not expressly cover logistics customs triage exposure.
The present record does not prove that final launch materials already contain the required explicit disclosure; it supports that such disclosure is required.
A clean compliance finding is not well supported on the current evidence.
